vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: local-voice
Version: 1.0.1

The skill establishes a local text-to-speech (TTS) and speech-to-text (STT) service on Apple Silicon. It uses standard macOS mechanisms like Homebrew for dependency installation (`espeak-ng`) and a LaunchAgent (`com.stella.voice.plist`) for user-level persistence, explicitly described in SKILL.md and implemented in scripts/setup.sh. The Swift application downloads its necessary AI models from its declared dependency (FluidAudio) and exposes a local HTTP API on 127.0.0.1:18790. All actions are transparently aligned with the stated purpose, and there is no evidence of data exfiltration, malicious execution, or prompt injection attempts against the agent.

llm.summary: This is a coherent local voice skill, but its default setup installs an always-running login service and lacks enough scoping and removal guidance for that persistent behavior.

dimensions.detail: A localhost HTTP daemon is proportionate for low-latency local voice features, but keeping it continuously available is broader than on-demand voice use requires.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The install script builds from compatible-version Swift dependencies, copies the result to ~/clawd/bin, removes/replaces an installed framework in that directory, and immediately loads the service.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: Setup instructions and scripts perform system-modifying shell actions, including Homebrew install, Swift build, binary/framework copying, and LaunchAgent loading, without a clear opt-in boundary or uninstall path.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The setup unconditionally creates a per-user LaunchAgent with RunAtLoad and KeepAlive for a user-writable installed binary, and the documentation/script use inconsistent service names.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: The artifacts consistently implement a local Apple Silicon TTS/STT HTTP daemon on 127.0.0.1:18790; the STT capability is present in the Swift daemon, not just advertised.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Install only if you are comfortable with a local voice daemon starting at login and staying alive in your user session. Before installing, review the LaunchAgent behavior, decide whether you want persistence, pin or review Swift dependencies, and make sure you have unload and removal steps for the plist and installed binary.
llm.findings:
[TP4] expected: Downgraded: full artifact inspection shows STT is implemented in sources/Sources/StellaVoice/main.swift via /transcribe, so the advertised TTS/STT purpose is not materially unsupported.
[TM1] expected: Downgraded: rm -rf is scoped to the installed ESpeakNG.framework under ~/clawd/bin and is used to replace a bundled framework during install, not to perform broad deletion.
[LP3] expected: Partially accepted: shell setup is expected for a local compiled daemon, but the lack of explicit scoping and warnings matters because installation also enables persistence.
[SQP-2] expected: Accepted as a Review concern: the LaunchAgent is purpose-aligned but defaults to persistent RunAtLoad and KeepAlive behavior without prominent warning or removal instructions.
[RA2] expected: Accepted in context: repeated RA2 instances describe the same LaunchAgent persistence; this is not malicious by itself, but it is under-controlled for a default setup path.
[E1] expected: Downgraded: the cited requests are to 127.0.0.1 for local TTS/STT or health checks, not evidence of off-host exfiltration.
[SSRF2] expected: Downgraded: loopback access is the advertised integration mechanism for the local daemon; the artifact does not show arbitrary internal host targeting.
[T06] expected: Accepted as material: scripts/setup.sh unconditionally registers and loads an always-on per-user LaunchAgent.
[T08] expected: Accepted as a supporting concern: Package.swift uses compatible-version dependency ranges and no inspected lockfile, which increases supply-chain risk for a binary that is then made persistent.
